mainTopic: מעשר בהמה: leftover animals, counting mistakes in the משנה, and whether the owner's count or the real order of the animals decides which one is holy
overview: This amud opens with a ברייתא that says you may not hand-pick ten animals for מעשר בהמה. You must run the flock through the pen, take the tenth, and let the leftovers join a later גורן. A second ברייתא about nineteen lambs says the leftovers are exempt. רב הונא בר סחורה resolves this with a pen that has two doors, where the last lamb could complete the ten at either door. He could not use simpler miscounting cases, because he holds that the real tenth animal becomes holy by itself. A new משנה then deals with counting mistakes: two animals coming out together, and an owner who mixes up the names of the ninth, tenth, and eleventh. In that משנה, רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה argue about whether the eleventh can make a תמורה. The גמרא then brings רבי יוחנן's rule about counting in pairs. רב מארי says the owner's count decides, and רב כהנא says the real number of animals decides. Each view is challenged and defended: רב כהנא by limiting the rule to deliberate pairs, and רב מארי by רבא's point that in Persian counting ten is called 'one'.

steps.title: No hand-picking ten; leftovers join a later round
steps.stepSummary: The end of a ברייתא rules that the owner must run the whole flock through the pen. The leftovers who were not counted toward a full ten are carried over to the next גורן.
steps.simpleTranslation: He may not say: 'I will choose ten, take one of them as tithe, and the rest will be exempt.' Instead, he brings them all into the pen, lets ten come out, takes one of them, and the rest join together with animals of another tithing round.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a ברייתא about how to do מעשר בהמה. It says you cannot shortcut by picking ten animals, and that animals left over are not exempt but wait for the next round.
steps.deeperAnalysis: מעשר בהמה only works by the animals passing through the opening of the pen and being counted. Picking ten by hand does not exempt the rest of the flock. The leftovers never finished a count of ten, so they are still obligated and get added to the next גורן.

keyTerms.meaning: he brings them into the pen
literally 'threshing floor'; here, a fixed time and round for tithing animals

steps.confusionAlert: This step starts in the middle of a ברייתא that began on the previous amud. The words 'לא יאמר' are its ruling, not a new opening.

phrases.english: He may not say: I will select ten
and I will take one of them (as tithe)
and the rest are exempt.
Rather, he brings them into the pen,
and lets ten go out (through the opening),
and takes one of them (the tenth),
and the remainder combine for another tithing round.
phrases.notes: The leftovers are still obligated and are counted with later animals.

steps.triggerLanguage: לֹא יֹאמַר: אֶבְרוֹר עֲשָׂרָה וְאֶטּוֹל מֵהֶן אֶחָד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues a ברייתא that began on the previous amud.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Tithing must be done by passing the animals through the pen. Leftovers that never completed a count of ten carry over to the next גורן.

steps.title: A second ברייתא says the leftovers are exempt
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא cites a ברייתא about nineteen lambs that uses the same procedure but rules that the remainder are fully exempt. This contradicts the first ברייתא.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it was taught: If he has nineteen lambs, he may not say, 'I will choose ten and take one of them, and the rest are exempt.' Rather, he brings them into the pen, lets ten out, takes one of them, and the rest are exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the first ברייתא by quoting another ברייתא that seems to say the opposite about the leftover animals.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both ברייתות agree that you must use the pen and not hand-pick. The conflict is only about the leftovers: the first says they join a later round, while this one says they are exempt. With nineteen lambs, the nine leftovers never seem to finish a count of ten, so why should they be exempt?

phrases.english: But it was taught: nineteen lambs,
he may not say: I will select ten
and take one of them,
and the rest are exempt.
Rather, he brings them into the pen,
and lets ten go out
and takes one of them,
and the remainder are exempt.
phrases.notes: This is the point of conflict with step 1.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Contradicts the ruling of step 1 about the leftovers.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that the leftovers join another גורן.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A parallel ברייתא with the same procedure rules that the leftovers are exempt, so the two sources contradict each other.

steps.title: A pen with two openings
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא בר סחורה explains the nineteen-lamb ברייתא as a pen with two doors. Nine lambs left through each door, and the last lamb could complete the ten at either one.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא בר סחורה explained it before רבא at the festival lecture: We are dealing with a pen that has two openings. Nine came out through this opening and nine through that opening, and the last one is fit to go out here or there.
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא בר סחורה answers the contradiction by limiting the second ברייתא to a special case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the last lamb could become the tenth for either line, both groups of nine were part of a count that could reach ten. So when the last lamb is taken as tithe, all the others count as exempted. The first ברייתא is about an ordinary pen, where leftovers who never could reach ten carry over to the next round.

keyTerms.meaning: at the festival (the public festival lecture)
fit for here and for there

steps.confusionAlert: Nine plus nine plus one equals nineteen. The lone last lamb can only walk out one door, but it could have become the tenth at either door. So both lines of nine were counting toward a possible ten, and that is why everyone is exempt.

phrases.english: Rav Huna bar Sechora interpreted it
before Rava at the festival lecture:

phrases.aramaic: בְּדִיר שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ שְׁנֵי פְתָחִים עָסְקִינַן,
phrases.english: We are dealing with a pen that has two openings,
and nine went out through this opening
and nine through that opening,
so that this last one
is fit (to complete the count) here and there.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּרְגְּמַהּ רַב הוּנָא בַּר סְחוֹרָה קַמֵּיהּ דְּרָבָא בְּרִיגְלָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 2.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case (אוקימתא): the second ברייתא is set in a special situation.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two ברייתות truly argue about leftover animals.
steps.terutzMaskana: The nineteen-lamb ברייתא is a two-door pen where every lamb was part of a count that could reach ten, so all are exempt. Otherwise the leftovers carry over.

steps.title: Why not a simpler case of miscounting?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רב הונא בר סחורה did not explain the case as counting nine, calling the tenth 'one', and restarting the count.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let him answer instead: For example, he counted nine, and when the tenth arrived he called it 'one' and started again from the beginning.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer by offering an easier explanation that would also make all nineteen exempt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With one door, he counts nine, mistakenly calls the tenth 'one', and counts on until the nineteenth lamb is called 'ten'. Then only the nineteenth is tithe, and all nineteen were in a count that reached ten, so all are exempt. Why did רב הונא need the unusual two-door pen?

keyTerms.meaning: let him answer it (this way instead)

phrases.english: But let him answer it:
for example, where he counted nine,
and when the tenth arrived
he called it 'one', starting from the beginning!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the choice of the two-door case in step 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא בר סחורה's choice of a two-door pen.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A simpler single-door case (miscounting the tenth as 'one') seems to produce the same result, so the unusual case looks unnecessary.

steps.title: The real tenth becomes holy by itself
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that רב הונא בר סחורה holds that the actual tenth animal becomes holy on its own, even if it is called 'one'. So the miscounting case would not work.
steps.simpleTranslation: He holds: the tenth becomes holy by itself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by showing that רב הונא בר סחורה has a different view of how the tenth becomes holy.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the tenth animal out of the pen is automatically holy, then calling it 'one' changes nothing. The real tenth is already tithe, so the count restarts after it, and the leftovers are not all exempt. That is why רב הונא needed the two-door case, where no single lamb is clearly the tenth until the end.

keyTerms.meaning: the tenth is sanctified by itself

steps.whatToRemember: The second ברייתא (leftovers exempt) is limited to a two-door pen. רב הונא בר סחורה could not use a miscounting case, because he holds that the true tenth animal becomes holy automatically, whatever name it is called.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that in מעשר בהמה, holiness comes from the animal's actual position as tenth, not only from what the owner says out loud.

phrases.english: He holds: the tenth is sanctified of its own accord.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 4 and defends step 3.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Pointing to the speaker's underlying view, which rules out the alternative case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Calling the tenth 'one' would push the tithe to the nineteenth lamb.
steps.terutzMaskana: The real tenth is holy on its own, so miscounting does not move the tithe, and the two-door case is needed.

steps.title: Why not explain it as counting in pairs?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רב הונא בר סחורה did not explain the nineteen-lamb ברייתא as a one-door pen where the owner counted the lambs two at a time.
steps.simpleTranslation: But he could have explained the case as a regular one-door pen at the gathering time, where the owner counted the lambs in pairs!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב הונא בר סחורה again. It offers another way he could have explained why the leftover lambs are exempt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Say the owner counts in pairs and calls each pair 'one', 'two', and so on. Then the nineteenth lamb would get the label 'ten' and become מעשר, and that would exempt the others. This seems simpler than imagining a pen with two doors, so why didn't he say it?

keyTerms.meaning: But let him answer / explain it as
The set gathering time for tithing animals (here: an ordinary pen with one door)
In pairs, two at a time

phrases.english: But let him explain it as a case of the gathering time (with a one-door pen),
phrases.notes: Meaning a normal pen, not a special pen with two doors.

phrases.english: where he counted them in pairs!
phrases.notes: Each pair gets one number, so the nineteenth lamb ends up called 'ten'.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second challenge of the same kind as Step 4: an alternative case setup that רב הונא בר סחורה could have used.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא בר סחורה's choice of the two-door pen explanation
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Counting in pairs would also make the nineteenth lamb 'ten' and exempt the rest. So the unusual two-door case seems unnecessary.

steps.title: The actual tenth animal by count is holy
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that רב הונא בר סחורה holds that the animal that is actually tenth in number becomes holy, no matter how the owner counts.
steps.simpleTranslation: He holds that the animal that is tenth in the real number of animals is the one that becomes holy.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from the previous step. It uses the same idea it used in Step 5.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Pairs do not change which animal is really tenth. The real tenth animal is in the fifth pair, and it becomes holy on its own. So pair-counting would not make the nineteenth lamb the מעשר, and that explanation does not work for him.

keyTerms.meaning: According to the real number of animals

phrases.english: He holds: the tenth by the count of animals
phrases.notes: What matters is the real number of animals, not the labels the owner uses.

phrases.english: is the one that is holy.

steps.triggerLanguage: קָסָבַר: עֲשִׂירִי לְמִנְיָן בְּהֵמוֹת הוּא קָדוֹשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 6 by applying the same principle used in Step 5.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Pointing to the speaker's underlying legal view
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Counting in pairs would make the nineteenth lamb the tenth.
steps.terutzMaskana: The real tenth animal (in the fifth pair) becomes holy automatically, so pair-counting cannot explain the ברייתא.

steps.title: Praise for רב הונא בר סחורה
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק praises רב הונא בר סחורה for explaining the ruling at the festival lecture exactly the way his teacher held.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק said: Fortunate is the mother of רב הונא בר סחורה, who explained the teaching at the festival lecture in line with the teacher's own view.
steps.whatsHappening: The discussion closes with a compliment. רב נחמן בר יצחק praises רב הונא בר סחורה for his answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב הונא בר סחורה's answer fit the teacher's own position, that the real tenth animal becomes holy, which is why רב נחמן בר יצחק praises it. This compliment closes the topic of the nineteen lambs.

keyTerms.meaning: Fortunate (worthy) is his mother, a phrase of praise
The festival (the public lecture given at festival time)
In line with his (the teacher's) own teaching

steps.whatToRemember: רב הונא בר סחורה explains the nineteen lambs as a pen with two doors because he holds that the real tenth animal is holy no matter how it is counted or named. His answer was praised for matching the teacher's view.

phrases.english: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said:

phrases.aramaic: זְכַאי אִימֵּיהּ דְּרַב הוּנָא בַּר סְחוֹרָה,
phrases.english: Fortunate is the mother of Rav Huna bar Sechora,
who explained the teaching to him
at the festival lecture, in line with his own teaching.

steps.triggerLanguage: זְכַאי אִימֵּיהּ דְּרַב הוּנָא בַּר סְחוֹרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the discussion by praising the answer that was just defended.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The two-door explanation stands, and it is praised for matching the teacher's view that the real tenth animal is holy.

steps.title: משנה: Two animals coming out together, and miscounting
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה rules that two animals coming out together are counted as two. If the owner counts two animals as 'one', his ninth and tenth are thrown off.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: If two animals came out together, he counts them as two. If he counted two of them as 'one', then the ninth and tenth are spoiled.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It deals with practical problems that come up while counting animals for מעשר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two animals leaving at once are each still counted one by one. If the owner accidentally gives two animals one number, every later number is off by one. The real tenth gets called 'ninth' and the eleventh gets called 'tenth', so the count is ruined at those spots.

phrases.english: MISHNA:
If two animals came out together,
he counts them as two (each one separately),
if he counted them as 'one',
the ninth and tenth are spoiled.
phrases.notes: The real tenth ends up called 'ninth', and the eleventh is called 'tenth'.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה about counting mistakes, a topic close to the discussion just finished.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Animals that come out together are still counted one by one. Counting two as 'one' spoils the ninth and tenth.

steps.title: Mixing up the ninth, tenth, and eleventh: רבי מאיר's ruling
steps.stepSummary: If the owner calls the ninth 'tenth', the tenth 'ninth', and the eleventh 'tenth', all three become holy, but each in a different way, according to רבי מאיר.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he called the ninth 'tenth', the tenth 'ninth', and the eleventh 'tenth', all three are holy. The ninth is eaten once it has a blemish. The tenth is מעשר. The eleventh is offered as a שלמים and can create a תמורה. These are the words of רבי מאיר.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה continues with a case where the owner gives the wrong names to animals nine, ten, and eleven. רבי מאיר rules what happens to each one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ninth becomes holy because it was called 'tenth', but it cannot be offered, so it is eaten only after it gets a blemish. The real tenth is true מעשר even though it was called 'ninth'. The eleventh, called 'tenth', becomes a שלמים offering with full status, so it can even make a swapped animal into a תמורה.

keyTerms.meaning: With its blemish (eaten only after it becomes blemished)
A substitute: an animal swapped for a holy animal, which itself becomes holy

steps.confusionAlert: Do not assume the tenth loses its holiness because it was called 'ninth'. It is still true מעשר, which matches the idea that the real tenth animal is holy. The wrong names only add holiness to the ninth and eleventh.
steps.whyThisMatters: This ruling shows that calling an animal 'tenth' can add holiness to it, while the real tenth stays holy regardless of its name.

phrases.english: If he called the ninth 'tenth',
and the tenth 'ninth',
and the eleventh 'tenth',
all three of them are holy:
the ninth is eaten once it has a blemish,
and the tenth is the tithe,
and the eleventh is offered as a peace offering
and it can create a substitute,
these are the words of Rabbi Meir.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה with another counting mistake: wrong names instead of a wrong count.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: All three are holy. The ninth is eaten once blemished, the tenth is מעשר, and the eleventh is a שלמים that can create a תמורה (רבי מאיר).

steps.title: רבי יהודה asks: can a substitute make a substitute?
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה challenges רבי מאיר's ruling that the eleventh animal, which was called 'tenth,' can make its own תמורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה said: Can a substitute (תמורה) make another substitute?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה objects to רבי מאיר's ruling from the previous step. רבי מאיר said the eleventh animal, which was wrongly called 'tenth,' becomes holy and can make its own תמורה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The eleventh animal only became holy because the owner called it by the tenth's name. So it looks like a substitute for the מעשר. A basic rule is that only an original קדשים animal can create a תמורה, and a substitute cannot create another substitute. So how can רבי מאיר say the eleventh makes a תמורה?

keyTerms.meaning: A substitute: an animal that becomes holy when someone tries to swap it for a holy animal
Can create a substitute: its own swap would take effect
'But is it really so?' A word that opens a challenging question

steps.confusionAlert: This is still part of the משנה, not the גמרא. רבי יהודה is arguing with רבי מאיר inside the משנה itself.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda said:
But is there a substitute that makes a substitute?
phrases.notes: He treats the eleventh animal as a substitute for the tenth.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רבי מאיר's ruling from Step 10 that the eleventh animal makes its own תמורה.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי מאיר's ruling that the eleventh animal called 'tenth' can create a תמורה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The eleventh is only a substitute for the tenth, and a substitute cannot create another substitute.

steps.title: Answer in רבי מאיר's name: it is offered, so it is not a real substitute
steps.stepSummary: The eleventh is not a true תמורה, because a real תמורה of מעשר is never offered, yet the eleventh is offered.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said in the name of רבי מאיר: If it were a substitute, it would not be offered on the altar.
steps.whatsHappening: The answer given in רבי מאיר's name is that the eleventh animal is not really a תמורה at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A real תמורה of מעשר is never brought on the altar. Yet רבי מאיר rules that the eleventh is offered as a שלמים. That shows it has its own independent holiness. Since it is not a substitute, it can create a תמורה of its own.

keyTerms.meaning: If it were so (a word that introduces an 'if... then' argument)

phrases.english: They said in the name of Rabbi Meir:
If it were a substitute,
it would not be offered.
phrases.notes: A substitute for מעשר is not brought on the altar, but the eleventh is.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִילּוּ הָיָה תְּמוּרָה לֹא הָיָה קָרֵב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבי יהודה's challenge from Step 11.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case: the eleventh has independent holiness and is not a substitute.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The eleventh is a substitute for the tenth, so it cannot create a תמורה.
steps.terutzMaskana: The eleventh is offered on the altar, which proves it is not a תמורה. So it can make a תמורה of its own.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the eleventh's holiness is its own kind of קדושה, not a copy of the tenth's.

steps.title: When the real tenth keeps its name, the eleventh is not holy
steps.stepSummary: If the owner calls the ninth, tenth, and eleventh all 'tenth,' the eleventh is not holy. The rule: if the real tenth was not stripped of the name 'tenth,' the eleventh does not become holy.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he called the ninth 'tenth,' the tenth 'tenth,' and the eleventh 'tenth,' the eleventh is not holy. This is the rule: whenever the name 'tenth' was not taken away from the real tenth, the eleventh is not holy.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives a new case and then a general rule. It explains exactly when the eleventh animal becomes holy and when it does not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 10, the real tenth was called 'ninth,' so it lost its name. Only then did the eleventh pick up holiness by being called 'tenth.' Here the real tenth was correctly called 'tenth,' so the name never left it. Calling the eleventh 'tenth' therefore does nothing.
steps.whatToRemember: The eleventh becomes holy only if the real tenth lost the name 'tenth.' If the real tenth was correctly called 'tenth,' the eleventh stays ordinary.

phrases.english: If he called the ninth 'tenth,'
and the tenth 'tenth,'
and the eleventh 'tenth,'
the eleventh is not holy.
This is the rule:

phrases.aramaic: כֹּל שֶׁלֹּא נֶעֱקַר שֵׁם עֲשִׂירִי מִמֶּנּוּ,
phrases.english: Whenever the name 'tenth' was not removed from it (the real tenth),
the eleventh is not holy.

steps.triggerLanguage: זֶה הַכְּלָל: כֹּל שֶׁלֹּא נֶעֱקַר שֵׁם עֲשִׂירִי מִמֶּנּוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Sets a limit on the case in Step 10 by showing when the eleventh does not become holy.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The eleventh called 'tenth' is holy only if the real tenth lost the name 'tenth.'

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: counting in pairs or in groups
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens with רבי יוחנן: if the owner counted the animals in pairs or in groups of a hundred, 'the tenth according to its count' is holy.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: If he counted them pair by pair, or hundred by hundred, the tenth according to its count is holy.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins with a new statement from רבי יוחנן about an owner who counts in groups instead of one animal at a time. Its wording, 'according to its count,' is unclear, and the next step asks about it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally each animal is counted on its own. רבי יוחנן says that counting in bigger units still works for מעשר. He does not say clearly which animal becomes the holy one, and that sets up the next question.

keyTerms.meaning: According to its count (the unclear phrase)

phrases.english: GEMARA:
Rabbi Yochanan said:
If he counted them pair by pair,
or hundred by hundred,
the tenth according to its count is holy.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: מְנָאָן זוּגוֹת זוּגוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא with a new ruling about counting in groups.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Counting in pairs or in groups still produces a holy tenth 'according to its count.'

steps.title: What does 'according to its count' mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what רבי יוחנן meant by the word 'לְמִנְיָנוֹ.'
steps.simpleTranslation: What does 'according to its count' mean?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what רבי יוחנן's unclear phrase means. This is a setup line that prepares for two different answers in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Its count' could mean the owner's count, or it could mean the actual number of animals. The answer decides which animals actually become holy.

phrases.english: 'According to its count' — what does it mean?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the meaning of a word in רבי יוחנן's ruling.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether 'its count' means the owner's count or the true number of animals.

steps.title: רב מארי and רב כהנא explain 'its count' differently
steps.stepSummary: רב מארי says it means the owner's own count. רב כהנא says it means the count of the animals themselves.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב מארי said: It is holy according to his own count. רב כהנא said: It is holy according to the number of animals.
steps.whatsHappening: Two אמוראים give opposite explanations of רבי יוחנן's phrase.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רב מארי, whatever unit the owner calls 'ten' is holy. For example, if he counts in pairs, the tenth pair (animals 19 and 20) is holy. According to רב כהנא, only the animal that is actually tenth in line is holy, no matter how he counted. This is the same idea רב הונא בר סחורה held in Step 7.

keyTerms.meaning: According to his own count (רב מארי)
According to the number of animals (רב כהנא)

steps.whatToRemember: רב מארי: the owner's count decides which animals are holy. רב כהנא: the true tenth animal is holy.

phrases.english: Rav Mari said:
It is holy according to his own count,
phrases.notes: Whatever group he calls 'ten' is holy.

phrases.english: Rav Kahana said:
It is holy according to the number of animals.
phrases.notes: Only the animal that is truly tenth is holy.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives two answers to the question in Step 15.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רב מארי: the owner's count. רב כהנא: the actual count of animals.
steps.whyThisMatters: The rest of this discussion tests which of these two readings fits the sources.

steps.title: Quoting the משנה about two animals coming out together
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes our משנה: two animals that come out together are counted as two, and if he counted them as 'one,' the ninth and tenth are ruined. It uses this to test the argument between רב מארי and רב כהנא.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned in the משנה: If two came out together, he counts them as two. If he counted them as one, the ninth and tenth are ruined.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes our own משנה from Step 9 to set up a test of the argument between רב מארי and רב כהנא. The actual argument from this משנה comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says that counting two animals as 'one' ruins the ninth and tenth. The animal he calls 'ninth' is really the tenth, and the one he calls 'tenth' is really the eleventh. One way to read it: the גמרא brings this to support רב מארי, because the owner's naming of the animals is what shapes the result.
steps.confusionAlert: This is the same משנה you already saw in Step 9. The גמרא is quoting it again on purpose, now as evidence in a new argument.

phrases.english: We learned in the Mishnah:
If two came out together,
he counts them as two.
If he counted them as one,
the ninth and tenth are ruined.
phrases.notes: He called the real tenth 'ninth' and the real eleventh 'tenth.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a source to test the argument in Step 16.
steps.raayaObject: רב מארי's view that the owner's count decides which animals are holy.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה (Step 9) about two animals coming out together and being counted as one.

steps.title: The משנה fits רב מארי but seems to challenge רב כהנא
steps.stepSummary: The משנה says the ninth and tenth are ruined when two animals came out together and were called by one number. That makes sense if the owner's count decides, as רב מארי says. It is hard to explain if the real count of the animals decides, as רב כהנא says.
steps.simpleTranslation: It works well for the one who says the animal is holy by the owner's own count. That is why the ninth and tenth are ruined: he called the real tenth 'ninth' and called the eleventh 'tenth.' But for the one who says it is holy by the real count of the animals, it should be as if he called the ninth 'ninth' and the tenth 'tenth.' So why are they ruined?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now uses the משנה from step 17 to attack רב כהנא. Two animals came out together and the owner gave them one number, so every name after that is off by one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רב מארי, the names matter. The real tenth animal got the name 'ninth,' and the eleventh got the name 'tenth,' so things are ruined. For רב כהנא, only the real order matters, so the real tenth should just be holy and nothing should be ruined. The משנה seems to go against him.

keyTerms.meaning: It works well for... (opens a contrast: this view fits, but the other does not)
by his own count, meaning the number the owner says (רב מארי)
by the count of the animals, meaning their real order (רב כהנא)
he calls it (gives it a name or number)

steps.confusionAlert: Picture it this way. Animals #9 and #10 walk out together, and the owner calls both of them 'nine.' Now the next animal, really #11, gets called 'ten.' The fight is over whether the owner's words count or the real order counts.

phrases.english: Granted, according to the one who says:
it is holy according to his own count,
phrases.notes: This is the view of רב מארי.

phrases.english: that is why they are
the ninth and tenth are ruined,
since he called the tenth 'ninth,'
and the eleventh 'tenth.'
But according to the one who says:
it is holy according to the count of the animals,
phrases.notes: This is the view of רב כהנא.

phrases.english: it is as if he called the ninth 'ninth,'
and called the tenth 'tenth'! (So why are they ruined?)

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּשְׁלָמָא לְמַאן דְּאָמַר לַמִּנְיָן שֶׁלּוֹ הוּא קָדוֹשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the test that step 17 began, showing that the משנה seems to fit רב מארי and not רב כהנא.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב כהנא's reading, that holiness follows the real count of the animals.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If only the real order matters, the owner's wrong names should not matter, so nothing should be ruined. Yet the משנה says the ninth and tenth are ruined.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן only meant a case of deliberate pairs
steps.stepSummary: For רב כהנא, רבי יוחנן limits his rule. The real count decides only when the owner chose on purpose to take the animals out in pairs. When two animals slipped out together by themselves and he miscounted, the real count does not decide.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן can tell you: when I said this, I meant a case where he intended to take them out in pairs. But where they came out by themselves, I did not say it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב כהנא by showing that the משנה is a different case from the one רבי יוחנן was talking about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן's rule is about an owner who planned to count by pairs or by hundreds. There we ignore his labels and follow the real order. The משנה is about animals that came out together by accident while the owner was counting one by one. In that case his mistaken name does matter, so the ninth and tenth are ruined.

keyTerms.meaning: he can say to you (the speaker is defended with an answer he could give)
he intended, he did it on purpose
in pairs, two at a time

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the owner's intent decides which counting rule applies. A planned counting system is treated differently from an accidental slip.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan can say to you:
When I said my rule,
I meant where he intended to take them out in pairs,
but where they came out by themselves, I did not say it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָךְ רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן כִּי אָמֵינָא אֲנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge against רב כהנא from step 18.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Case distinction, meaning the rule is limited to a narrower case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought רבי יוחנן's rule covers every time two animals come out together.
steps.terutzMaskana: The rule covers only counting in pairs on purpose. An accidental double exit with a wrong name ruins the ninth and tenth, as the משנה says.

steps.title: Counting backward seems to challenge רב מארי
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says that if the owner counted backward, the tenth animal in the line is holy, even though he called it 'one.' This fits רב כהנא but seems hard for רב מארי.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: if he counted them backward, the tenth in the line is holy. That works well for the one who says it is holy by the count of the animals. But for the one who says it is holy by the owner's count, he called the tenth 'one'!
steps.whatsHappening: Now the גמרא brings a new source that goes the other way. It challenges רב מארי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When counting backward (ten, nine, eight, and so on), the tenth animal to come out gets the name 'one.' רב כהנא is fine, because it really is the tenth animal. רב מארי says the owner's number decides, and the owner said 'one,' not 'ten.' So how can it be holy?

phrases.english: Come and hear:
if he counted them backward,
the tenth in the line is holy.
Granted, according to the one who says
it is holy by the count of the animals, this works well,
but according to the one who says
it is holy by his own count,
he called the tenth 'one'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Now that רב כהנא has been defended, the גמרא turns to a source that challenges the other side, רב מארי.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב מארי's reading, that holiness follows the owner's own count.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The owner named the tenth animal 'one,' yet the ברייתא says it is holy. That suggests the real order decides, not the name.

steps.title: רבא: in Persian counting, ten is called 'one'
steps.stepSummary: רבא defends רב מארי. In Persian counting, a group of ten is called 'one,' so calling the tenth animal 'one' can still count as calling it the tenth.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: since in Persian counting they call ten 'one,' the name 'one' can mean tenth.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge to רב מארי, so both opinions are still standing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב מארי still holds that the owner's name matters. The word 'one' has a known meaning of 'ten,' because Persians count in units of ten. So the owner's name and the real tenth animal do not clash, and the animal is holy.
steps.whatToRemember: Both sides survive. רב כהנא (real count decides) is saved by limiting רבי יוחנן's rule to deliberate pairs. רב מארי (the owner's count decides) is saved because 'one' can mean ten in Persian counting.

phrases.english: Rava said:
Since it exists in Persian counting,
that they call ten 'one.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא הוֹאִיל וְאִיתֵיהּ בְּמִנְיָנָא פָּרְסָאָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge against רב מארי from step 20.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation of wording, meaning the name 'one' can also mean 'ten.'
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Calling the tenth animal 'one' is a name that does not match, so for רב מארי it should not be holy.
steps.terutzMaskana: In Persian counting, 'one' means a unit of ten, so the name fits the tenth and it is holy even for רב מארי.
